title: Nkate Cake
author: Kelly Cletheroe
desc: Two hundred grams of roasted peanuts into caramelised sugar — stir quickly, because the mixture will begin to stiffen.
longDesc: Peanut brittle, Ghanaian style, sold in slabs and triangles at every lorry park. Two hundred grams of roasted unsalted peanuts are chopped with a large knife or a food processor. A hundred and fifty grams of granulated sugar melts in a steel pan over low heat, stirring occasionally, which may take a few minutes. Once the sugar has turned golden brown and has no more lumps, the chopped peanuts go in and you stir quickly to coat them, because the mixture will begin to stiffen. It is poured onto greaseproof paper, flattened under a second sheet, and cut while hot — watch your fingers, because it will still be very hot.
ingredients: 200 g (1 1/3 cups) roasted unsalted peanuts, without shells
equipment: Rolling pin or flat-based pan, to flatten
steps: Chop the peanuts, using a large knife or a food processor.
Put the sugar in a medium or large steel pan over low heat.
Allow the sugar to melt, stirring occasionally. This may take a few minutes.
Once the sugar has turned golden brown and has no more lumps, pour the chopped peanuts into the pan.
Stir quickly to coat the peanuts with the caramel, as the mixture will begin to stiffen.
Pour it onto a baking tray lined with greaseproof paper.
Top with a second sheet and flatten. Watch your fingers, as the mixture will still be VERY hot.
chefTips: Golden brown AND no more lumps. Both conditions, and the lumps are the one people miss — undissolved sugar gives a grainy brittle.
Low heat, not medium. Sugar alone with no water scorches fast and there is no recovering it.
Stir quickly once the nuts go in, because it begins to stiffen immediately. Have the tray and paper ready before you start.
Cut it while hot. Cold brittle shatters where it wants to, not where you score it.
The second sheet of greaseproof is what lets you press it flat without burning yourself. Use a rolling pin on top of it.
Double the quantities for a bigger batch, by the author's own note. The ratio holds.
Best fresh, though it keeps a week airtight. Humidity is what makes brittle go sticky.
commonMistakes: Medium or high heat, which burns the sugar.
Adding the nuts before the lumps have gone.
Stirring slowly once the nuts are in.
Pressing it flat with a bare hand.
sources: Adapted from 'Nkate Cake – Desserts of the World', maverickbaking.com. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'by Kelly', author page slug kellycletheroe — the surname comes from the slug and not from the byline line, which prints a first name only. Date: 14 September 2022. Yield as printed: 'Persons 16'. All figures TWO-PASS.
Ingredients exactly as printed: '200g (1 ⅓ cup) roasted unsalted peanuts (without shells)'; '150g (¾ cup) granulated sugar'. Two ingredients, nothing else.

Method as printed, in order: chop the peanuts 'using a large knife or a food processor'; sugar in a 'medium/large steel pan' over 'low heat'; 'Allow the sugar to melt, stirring occasionally. This may take a few minutes.'; 'Once the sugar has turned golden brown and has no more lumps, pour the chopped peanuts into the pan.'; 'Stir quickly to coat the peanuts with the caramel as the mixture will begin to stiffen.'; pour onto a lined baking tray; top with a second sheet and flatten — 'Watch your fingers as the mixture will still be VERY hot!'; cut while hot; 'Allow to cool completely.'
THE DONENESS CUE, verbatim and two-part: 'Once the sugar has turned golden brown and has no more lumps'. Both conditions are printed and both are reproduced.
TIPS as printed: 'you can double this recipe's quantities for a bigger batch'; and it 'will keep well in an airtight container for up to 1 week but is best enjoyed fresh.'

A SOURCING FLAG, stated rather than hidden: THE AUTHOR IS A WESTERN HOME BAKER, not a Ghanaian cook, and the page presents nkate cake as a Ghanaian street food in a 'Desserts of the World' series. NO GHANAIAN-AUTHORED NKATE CAKE RECIPE WITH QUANTITIES WAS FOUND. This is the only source in the material consulted that meets the collection's bar — named author, full quantities, an observable doneness cue — and its non-Ghanaian authorship is disclosed here rather than obscured.

A SOURCE REJECTED: a 'nkate cake inspired cashew candy bar' on yummymedley.com has no byline and no date, and uses CASHEWS rather than groundnuts, with ½ cup sugar, 1 cup toasted cashews and ¼ tsp salt at a ¼-inch roll-out. It is not a groundnut recipe and is not used.

A POINTER ONLY, not a source: the Wikipedia 'Nkatie cake' article lists ½ cup sugar, ½ cup roasted groundnut and 1 tsp vegetable oil, citing the Yummy Medley cashew page above, which could not be read. ITS RATIO DISAGREES WITH THIS RECIPE'S — roughly 1:1 sugar to nuts against this recipe's 150 g sugar to 200 g nuts — and the two are NOT reconciled. Its page also makes no claim about Akan origin.

AN EMPTY SEARCH, recorded: no recipe for nkate or peanut sweets under their Twi names (nkatie, nkate toffee, groundnut candy) was retrievable from a named Ghanaian author. Whitby's 1968 CSIR-FRI survey has no passage on nkate sweets at all, covering only groundnut soup, groundnut oil and kulikuli.

COMMUNITY NOT ESTABLISHED: nothing in the sources attributes nkate cake to a particular Ghanaian ethnic group, so it is filed as national rather than assigned one. 'Nkate' is the Twi word for groundnut, which is suggestive but not evidence.

RELATED PREPARATIONS in this collection, from one nut: kuli-kuli as de-oiled pressed cakes (GHA072), tankora as the powder made from them (GHA064), dzowoe as uncooked spiced peanut balls (GHA092), spicy coated groundnuts as a battered fried snack (GHA108), and the groundnut toffee at GHA117, which is a different and Ghanaian-sourced treatment of the same brittle idea.
storage: Up to a week in an airtight container, per the author. Best fresh.
healthBenefits: Peanuts supply protein, niacin, folate, magnesium and vitamin E.
Just two ingredients, with no additives or preservatives.
The nuts outweigh the sugar, which is unusual for a brittle.
culturalNote: Nkate cake is sold in plastic-wrapped slabs through car windows at every Ghanaian traffic junction, and it is the one Ghanaian sweet most visitors come home talking about. That the only retrievable recipe with real quantities is by a British home baker rather than a Ghanaian cook says something about whose food gets written down.
